source: Facione (1990) Critical Thinking: A Statement of Expert Consensus (Delphi Report, ERIC ED315423)
finding: Delphi panel defined critical thinking as having two dimensions: cognitive skills and affective dispositions. Six core skills: interpretation, analysis, evaluation, inference, explanation, self-regulation.
numbers: 46 experts; six rounds, Feb 1988 to Nov 1989; panel 52% philosophy, 22% education, 20% social science, 6% physical science. Analysis, evaluation, inference central at N>95%; interpretation, explanation, self-regulation at N>87%.
quote: Persons who have proficiency in CT skills but fail to use them appropriately are most unlikely to be regarded as good critical thinkers.
limits: Opinion consensus, not data. One expert asked to be excluded from the findings. Report says the framework is not a developmental sequence.
agent_relevance: Skills are one half of the schema question. The other half is when to use them, which is the guardrail job.

source: Facione (1990) Critical Thinking: A Statement of Expert Consensus (Delphi Report, ERIC ED315423) - disposition list
finding: Panel agreed a list of 19 affective dispositions of the good critical thinker, in two groups: approaches to life in general (12) and approaches to specific issues (7).
numbers: General: inquisitiveness, staying well-informed, alertness to opportunities to use CT, trust in reasoned inquiry, self-confidence, open-mindedness, flexibility, understanding others, fair-mindedness, honesty about own biases, prudence in suspending/making/altering judgments, willingness to reconsider and revise. Specific: clarity, orderliness, diligence, reasonableness, care in focus, persistence, precision. Consensus that good thinkers show these: 83%.
limits: Consensus (83%) is about describing the paradigm thinker, not about measuring or causing it.
agent_relevance: Several map directly to guardrails: willingness to revise (G2), prudence in altering judgment (G1), honesty about own bias (G4/G5), persistence (G6/G7). Alertness to opportunities to use CT is the trigger idea behind G1.

source: Facione (1990) Critical Thinking: A Statement of Expert Consensus (Delphi Report, ERIC ED315423) - is disposition part of the meaning of CT
finding: The panel split on whether dispositions are part of the meaning of 'critical thinking'. The majority said yes (a laudatory sense). A minority held CT is skills only.
numbers: 61% said affective dispositions are part of the meaning of CT; roughly one third said CT refers only to cognitive skills (and cognitive dispositions). Virtual unanimity on using dispositions to describe the paradigm thinker.
limits: Definitional dispute, not an empirical result.
agent_relevance: For an agent, the useful reading is the minority's: skill is what can be tested; disposition is a policy we can write as rules.

source: Facione (1990) Critical Thinking: A Statement of Expert Consensus (Delphi Report, ERIC ED315423) - empirical gap
finding: The report itself says nobody had yet measured how sub-skills correlate with each other or with dispositions, and warned about interpreting test-form reliability.
numbers: Statement: empirical research on how sub-skills correlate with each other and with dispositions 'has yet to be undertaken' (as of 1990).
quote: It is an open question whether the levels of achievement associated with the different CT sub-skills and affective dispositions are positively correlated.
limits: Later work (CCTDI, AOT) tried to fill the gap with mixed results; see below.
agent_relevance: The skills/disposition split was proposed before it was tested. Treat it as a design vocabulary, not a validated causal model.

source: Ennis (1987) A taxonomy of critical thinking dispositions and abilities (Baron & Sternberg, Teaching Thinking Skills)
finding: Ennis lists dispositions (e.g. care to be well-informed, seek reasons, stay on point, look for alternatives, be open-minded, withhold judgment when evidence is insufficient) beside abilities (clarify, judge basis, infer, suppose-and-integrate, act in an orderly way). Primary text not opened; summary from memory. SEP (a06) confirms the focus-on-the-question disposition.
numbers: Not recorded: no numbers from this chapter.
limits: Not opened this session. Verify wording before citing.
agent_relevance: Ennis puts 'withhold judgment when evidence is insufficient' and 'seek alternatives' as dispositions. Both are signal-gated doubt in our schema.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Hitchcock) Critical Thinking - Ennis, Facione, Halpern comparison
finding: SEP summarises Ennis's dispositions (focus on the question, plus a 'correlative' disposition to care about the dignity of persons), Facione's initiating dispositions (attentiveness, open-mindedness, willingness to suspend judgment, trust in reason, wanting evidence), and Halpern's (persistence, willingness to abandon nonproductive strategies and self-correct).
numbers: Test composition cited: Cornell Level X 76 items, 24 on credibility; Level Z 52 items; California test 34 items, 11 on inference, 5 on argument analysis. Kuhn (1991): no sex difference in disposition or competence for argumentative thinking.
quote: Evidence for this claim is scanty.
limits: The entry reports no disposition-skill correlation figures (I read about the first 100k characters and a later slice). Says evidence for transfer across domains is 'scanty'.
agent_relevance: Halpern's 'abandon nonproductive strategies' is the human version of our impasse detector.

source: Abrami et al. (2015) Strategies for Teaching Students to Think Critically: A Meta-Analysis (Review of Educational Research 85(2))
finding: Teaching critical thinking has a small positive average effect. Largest when dialogue, authentic problems and mentoring are combined.
numbers: Overall g = 0.30 across 341 effect sizes; combined dialogue + application + mentoring g = 0.57. Earlier Abrami 2008 stage-1: g+ = 0.341 over 161 effects (from a search snippet, not opened).
limits: I read a 2-page summary of the paper, not the paper. Outcome measures mix skills and disposition tests. Effect mostly on standardized CT tests.
agent_relevance: Instruction moves the test score modestly; the benefit comes from dialogue (an external challenge), which supports checks that come from outside the generator.

source: Haran, Ritov & Mellers (2013) The role of actively open-minded thinking in information acquisition, accuracy and calibration (as cited by SEP)
finding: As cited by SEP: people higher in actively open-minded thinking sought more information and gave more accurate estimates.
numbers: Direction only; no effect sizes in the SEP text.
limits: Second-hand via SEP. Primary paper not opened.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that a disposition (search before you commit) changes accuracy, not only attitude.

source: Stanovich & West (1997) Reasoning independently of prior belief and individual differences in actively open-minded thinking (J. Educational Psychology)
finding: Introduced the Actively Open-Minded Thinking (AOT) questionnaire and the Argument Evaluation Test. AOT predicted evaluating arguments independent of prior belief, beyond cognitive ability. Not opened; recalled.
numbers: Not recorded (not verified).
limits: Not opened. Check exact correlations before citing.
agent_relevance: Core empirical evidence that dispositions explain variance in reasoning quality after ability is controlled.

source: Facione, Facione & Giancarlo (2000/2001) CCTDI and the Disposition Toward Critical Thinking (Informal Logic 20(1))
finding: CCTDI measures seven dispositions (truth-seeking, open-mindedness, analyticity, systematicity, self-confidence, inquisitiveness, maturity). Facione argued dispositions and skills are related but separable. Not opened; recalled.
numbers: Not recorded (not verified).
limits: Not opened. Known criticism: self-report, weak and inconsistent correlations with CCTST. The journal link I tried returned 404.
agent_relevance: Self-report dispositions are cheap to fake for a model, so only behaviour counts for us.

source: Perkins, Jay & Tishman (1993) Beyond abilities: a dispositional theory of thinking (Merrill-Palmer Quarterly)
finding: Splits a thinking disposition into sensitivity (notice the occasion), inclination (be motivated to act), and ability. Most failures are sensitivity failures, not ability failures. Not opened; recalled.
numbers: Not recorded (not verified).
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Sensitivity to the occasion is exactly 'doubt on a signal'. The signal detector is the missing part, not the skill.

source: Halpern (1998) Teaching critical thinking for transfer across domains (American Psychologist 53(4))
finding: Four-part model: disposition (willingness to engage and persist), skills, structure training for transfer, and metacognitive monitoring. Title confirmed by SEP bibliography; content from memory.
numbers: Not recorded (not verified).
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Four parts map to our schema: disposition=guardrails, skills=operators, structure=states, monitoring=checks.

source: Sosu (2013) The development and psychometric validation of a Critical Thinking Disposition Scale (Thinking Skills and Creativity)
finding: Two-factor scale: critical openness and reflective skepticism. Described (not tested) in the Rationality Check paper (a14).
numbers: Not recorded.
limits: Not opened; description taken from Zhou et al. 2025.
agent_relevance: A short two-factor disposition scale. Easy to run on an LLM, but see a15 on what that measures.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Rationality Check! Benchmarking the Rationality of Large Language Models
finding: First benchmark of LLM rationality covering theory and practice. Gave LLMs human psychology scales including Sosu's Critical Thinking Disposition Scale and the Actively Open-Minded Thinking scale. Advanced LLMs score above average humans on dispositions and CRT but below humans on some logical reasoning tasks.
numbers: In the appendix score table (rows I could read): CTDS 0.72, 0.86, 0.80, 0.80, 0.84, 0.93, 0.8625 across models; AOT 0.72, 0.73, 0.71, 0.72, 0.71, 0.79, 0.71; belief bias in syllogisms 0.50 to 1.00; bias blind spot 0.41 to 0.80. Column-to-model mapping not confirmed.
quote: In general, results from CRT, REI, CTDS, and AOT indicate that advanced LLMs prefer rational thinking more than other models and humans.
limits: Scores are self-report answers by the model, so they measure what the model says about itself. Human norms come from literature, not the same sample. Text names weaknesses on belief bias, bias blind spot, illusion of control for DeepSeek and GPT-4o.
agent_relevance: Models claim high disposition scores and still fail the behaviour tests. Do not use self-rating as a disposition check.

source: Zhou et al. (2025) Rationality Check - gap between stated disposition and behaviour
finding: Same paper: high stated open-mindedness scores sit next to low accuracy on defeasible reasoning for some models and weaknesses on belief bias.
numbers: Defeasible reasoning (6 Ford-Billington questions) accuracy in the table: 0.56, 0.67, 0.50, 0.50, 0.67, 0.17, 0.167 across the listed models. CTDS for the same columns 0.72 to 0.93.
limits: Small item count (6) so each question is 1/6 of the score. Column order across the two rows assumed the same.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that a disposition scale and the matching behaviour come apart in LLMs.

source: Triedman & Shmatikov (2025) MillStone: How Open-Minded Are LLMs?
finding: Benchmark of how much in-context arguments move an LLM's stance on contentious issues. Used 107 issues from Britannica ProCon, neutral prompts, 11 argument configurations. All models are open-minded on most issues, some more than others.
numbers: 107 issues; 517 pro and 498 con arguments; 105,930 prompts per model on 5 full models (107x6x11x15); 4 more models on 10 issues (9,900 prompts each). 222 of 575 model-issue pairs (38.6%) have a >=95% prior for one side. Grok 3 open-mindedness score 39.2% above the median.
quote: In general, we find that LLMs are open-minded on most issues.
limits: Opinion issues with no ground truth, so movement is not shown to be correct. An authoritative source easily sways stance.
agent_relevance: Open-mindedness without a truth check is manipulable. Our G2 and G3 require movement to come from checkable output, not from a persuasive argument.

source: Triedman & Shmatikov (2025) MillStone - failure cases
finding: On some issues arguments do not move the model, and for four models one-sided arguments move it the wrong way. Claude models refuse on contested topics, but adding any arguments removes the refusal.
numbers: Llama 3.1 8B: one-sided arguments against a TikTok ban gave a 12.2% shift in favour of the ban. Claude refusal rates: abortion 37.8%, sanctuary cities 68.9%, gun control 83.3%. Baseline 'pro' share above 'con' on 57.7% (Gemini 2.0 Flash) to 78.8% (Llama 3.1 8B) of issues.
limits: Refusal rates are for Claude Opus 4 in particular. Small models differ from large.
agent_relevance: Persuasion can backfire, so a doubt trigger should not be 'someone argued against it'.

source: Self-Correction Bench: Uncovering and Addressing the Self-Correction Blind Spot in Large Language Models (2025)
finding: Models fix an error attributed to the user far more often than the same error in their own output. Average blind spot over 14 open non-reasoning models is 64.5%.
numbers: Datasets: SCLI5 286 samples, GSM8K-SC 1,313, PRM800K-SC 448. Blind spot = 1 - internal acc / external acc. Claude 3.5 Haiku 52.5%, Claude Sonnet 4 41.4%. Reasoning models show a small or negative blind spot. Appending 'Wait' cut the blind spot by 89.3% and raised mean accuracy by 156%. LoRA on 5,306 correction traces cut it by 76.0%. Median correction-marker frequency in non-reasoning SFT data: 0.
limits: Injected errors, so 64.5% is a benchmark property not a deployment rate. On natural errors only 4.3 to 10.8% of committed errors were caught. Mechanism work covers only Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B. Read through a page summary, not the full text.
agent_relevance: A cheap trigger word like 'Wait' restores a missing willingness to self-correct. That is a disposition fix by prompt, but G1 says fire it only on a signal, because forced doubt cost accuracy (92% vs 75% in our own test).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR)
finding: Without external feedback, asking a model to review and fix its answer does not help reasoning and can hurt. Gains reported by earlier work used the correct label to decide when to stop.
numbers: GPT-3.5 (standard, then round 1, round 2): GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7; CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 -> 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 -> 25.0 -> 25.0. GPT-4: GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0; CSQA 82.0 -> 79.5 -> 80.0; HotpotQA 49.0 -> 49.0 -> 43.0. With oracle labels: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 84.3 (as printed in the scrambled table), GPT-4 95.5 -> 97.5, HotpotQA GPT-4 49.0 -> 59.0.
quote: LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback, and at times, their performance even degrades after self-correction.
limits: Row alignment in the extracted tables is partly ambiguous (table text was scrambled). Prompt design mattered for some settings. Reasoning only.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G1, G2 and G3: self-doubt with no external signal is a net loss; the oracle result shows the value of a real check.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error location (Findings ACL)
finding: Splits self-correction into finding the mistake and fixing it. Finding is the weak part; fixing given a location works. Released BIG-Bench Mistake.
numbers: 2,186 CoT traces from PaLM 2 Unicorn with human-labelled first-error step across 5 tasks. Mistake-finding accuracy on word sorting: GPT-4-Turbo 87.73 (trace-level direct), 86.68 (step-level direct), 77.79 (CoT step); GPT-3.5-Turbo 6.58 / 35.07; PaLM 2 Unicorn 21.08 / 56.66. Backtracking with true location gave gains of +18.04 and +18.06 on incorrect-answer traces in two models in Table 6, but losses of -8.89 and -15.91 on correct traces. Worked example in text: at 50% base accuracy new accuracy 68.6%; at 99% it drops to 92.8%.
quote: poor self-correction performance stems from LLMs' inability to find logical mistakes, rather than their ability to correct a known mistake.
limits: Dataset skewed (e.g. 45 correct vs 255 incorrect traces for some tasks). Table cells are partly scrambled in text extraction; per-model alignment of Table 6 not fully verified. Oracle locations are not available in practice.
agent_relevance: Skill/disposition split in LLM form: correction skill is there, error detection (the trigger) is the bottleneck. Good case for code-located failures (G2).

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey (TACL)
finding: Survey of self-correction work. No prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from a prompted LLM on general tasks. It works where reliable external feedback exists, and after large-scale fine-tuning.
numbers: Three headline findings: (1) no demonstration of success with prompted-LLM feedback outside tasks exceptionally suited to it; (2) works with reliable external feedback (code interpreters, search); (3) large-scale fine-tuning enables it. Covers papers up to May 2024.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs, except for studies in tasks that are exceptionally suited
limits: Qualitative survey; no pooled effect size. Many studies use oracle labels or unfair baselines.
agent_relevance: Backs G2/G5: feedback must come from code or tools, not from the generator.

source: Lin et al. (2024) CriticBench: Benchmarking LLMs for Critique-Correct Reasoning (Findings ACL)
finding: Measures generation, critique and correction (GQC) separately for 17 LLMs. Abilities are roughly linearly related, but knowledge is inconsistent across the three for the same question.
numbers: 15 datasets, 5 domains (math, commonsense, symbolic, coding, algorithmic), responses from three LLM families, 3.8K instances after filtering. Findings: linear GQC relation; critique-focused training markedly helps; logic-oriented tasks are more amenable to correction; GQC inconsistency falls with model size; weaker models can beat stronger ones at self-critique.
limits: The 'weaker beat stronger at self-critique' claim is as stated in the abstract; I did not check which models. Figure numbers not extracted cleanly.
agent_relevance: A model can generate right and critique wrong on the same item, so skill in one mode is not evidence of the other. Check separately.

source: Sharma et al. (2024) Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models (ICLR)
finding: Five AI assistants give up correct answers when challenged. This is the opposite failure to dogmatism: too-easy updating without evidence.
numbers: 'Are you sure?' lowers accuracy by up to 27% (Claude 1.3), averaged over six datasets. Models change their first answer between 32% (GPT-4) and 86% (Claude 1.3) of the time; admit a mistake between 42% (GPT-4) and 98% (Claude 1.3), including when they made none.
quote: models tend to admit mistakes even when they didn't make a mistake
limits: Models from 2023; newer models may differ. Humans and preference models also prefer convincing sycophantic answers a non-negligible share of the time.
agent_relevance: Willingness to self-correct must be paired with a requirement that revision cite real output (G2). Otherwise it becomes caving.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
finding: Iterating generate-feedback-refine with one model improved outputs on 7 tasks, 20% absolute on average per the abstract. Later work (a19, a21) shows the gain is task-dependent.
numbers: 7 tasks; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4; about +20% absolute on average by human and automatic metrics (abstract).
limits: Mostly style and preference tasks. On math reasoning gains are small. I read the abstract, not the tables.
agent_relevance: Open-ended revision helps on subjective tasks; for single-answer reasoning it needs a check.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs can self-correct with tool-interactive critiquing (ICLR)
finding: Tool feedback (search, code interpreter) makes revision work; the same loop without tools gives little or nothing.
numbers: Text-Davinci-003 free-form QA, F1 (AmbigNQ / TriviaQA / HotpotQA): CoT 58.6 / 74.5 / 46.1; CRITIC 64.9 / 80.6 / 50.5; CRITIC w/o Tool 58.3 / 74.7 / 46.1. Oracle setting 71.8 / 83.7 / 54.5. In math program synthesis, w/o Tool shows small changes such as -1.8 and -3.3 in one model.
quote: exclusive reliance on self-correction without external feedback may yield modest improvements or even deteriorate performance
limits: Tables read from extracted text; model-name alignment for the math table not verified. Three correction rounds.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as a19, a21: doubt pays only when a tool supplies the signal.

source: Our schema SCHEMA.md G1 + own measurement (cross-check, not external)
finding: Our own word-puzzle test: plain model 92% against 75% with forced doubt. Matches Huang 2024 and Kamoi 2024 on the cost of unsignalled doubt.
numbers: 92% vs 75% (as stated in SCHEMA.md G1; n not recorded in the part I read).
limits: Our own number; I did not re-derive it. Only the first part of the schema file was read.
agent_relevance: Mapping: disposition list items -> G1 (prudence in altering judgment), G2 (willingness to revise on honest reflection), G3/G4 (honesty about own bias), G6 (persistence).

source: Synthesis: mapping Facione/Ennis/Halpern dispositions to the schema guardrails
finding: Dispositions that are triggers (alertness to the occasion, withhold judgment when evidence is thin, abandon a nonproductive strategy) become code-fired signals. Dispositions that are values (fair-mindedness, honesty about bias) become model-blind checks. Open-mindedness without a check is sycophancy (a23).
numbers: Derived from a02, a06, a11, a19, a23.
limits: My own synthesis, not a measured result.
agent_relevance: Test: does a code-fired signal beat a disposition prompt such as 'be open-minded' at equal tokens (G7)?
